title: Type 1 diabetes: targets, insulin and self-management
blurb: Recognise type 1 diabetes, know the NICE NG17 glucose and HbA1c targets, and support safe basal-bolus insulin, injection technique and hypo awareness.
question: Ms Duarte, 26, has type 1 diabetes and uses capillary testing. Her readings this week are 9.8 on waking, 6.2 before lunch and 6.8 before her evening meal. Which reading is outside the NICE target, and why?

teach.body: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition in which the pancreas stops making insulin, so lifelong insulin replacement is essential. People typically (but not always) present with ketosis, rapid weight loss, onset under 50, BMI below 25, or a personal or family history of autoimmune disease. NICE warns not to use age or BMI alone to rule it in or out. Plain English: without insulin, the body burns fat for fuel and makes ketones, so insulin is never optional.

teach.caption: Targets are individualised (1.6.7) and must not come at the cost of problematic hypoglycaemia (1.6.8).

teach.h: Type 1 versus type 2 at a glance
Basal-bolus insulin is the regimen of choice
teach.body: NICE recommends multiple daily injection basal-bolus insulin for all adults with type 1 diabetes: a long-acting (basal) insulin covers background needs, and rapid-acting (bolus) insulin is matched to each meal. Do not offer newly diagnosed adults twice-daily mixed, basal-only or bolus-only regimens. Structured education such as DAFNE (dose adjustment for normal eating) is offered 6–12 months after diagnosis.

steps.label: Rotate sites
steps.sub: Avoid repeated injections at the same point

teach.caption: NICE NG17 recs 1.7.19–1.7.21. Unexplained highs and lows: look at the injection sites.

a day when ill, before driving, around sport
offer a choice of real-time or intermittently scanned
hypoglycaemia awareness check (Gold or Clarke score)

teach.text: Do not relax glucose targets to fix impaired hypoglycaemia awareness. NICE says avoid relaxing targets; instead, check structured education, review insulin, and consider a pump or real-time CGM. Relaxed targets are a type 2 frailty idea (NG28), not the NG17 answer to unawareness.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Petrov in the diabetes clinic
teach.body: Mr Petrov, 34, has type 1 diabetes. His HbA1c is 61 mmol/mol and he has had several unexplained lows. The nurse finds firm lumps at his abdominal injection sites where he always injects. She explains lipohypertrophy, teaches site rotation, and checks his hypo awareness with a Gold score. She also reminds him of sick-day rules: check ketones when unwell and never stop basal insulin.

children.label: IM glucagon by a trained relative or friend

items: HbA1c 48 mmol/mol or lower, individualised, without problematic hypos.
Capillary glucose 5–7 on waking and 4–7 before meals; test at least 4 times a day.
Basal-bolus is the regimen of choice; DAFNE-style education 6–12 months after diagnosis.
Rotate sites; check them at least annually for lipohypertrophy.
Assess hypo awareness annually (Gold or Clarke); ketone testing is part of sick-day rules.

summary: You can now recognise the typical features of type 1 diabetes and apply the NG17 HbA1c and capillary glucose targets. You can also support basal-bolus insulin, injection site care, monitoring and hypoglycaemia awareness so the person can self-manage safely.

A.q: Ms Duarte, 26, has type 1 diabetes and tests her capillary glucose. Which waking (fasting) reading falls within the NICE NG17 target?
A.why: NICE NG17 rec 1.6.22: aim for 5–7 mmol/L on waking. 6.1 is within range.

whyNot.0: 3.8 mmol/L is below 4.0, a hypoglycaemia level, and below the 5–7 waking target.
whyNot.2: 8.4 mmol/L is above the 5–7 waking target.
whyNot.3: 10.2 mmol/L is well above the waking target.

A.q: Mr Kamara, 30, was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes last week. Which insulin regimen does NICE recommend as the regimen of choice?
A.why: NICE NG17 recs 1.7.1–1.7.2: offer multiple daily injection basal-bolus regimens; do not offer newly diagnosed adults twice-daily mixed, basal-only or bolus-only regimens.

whyNot.0: Twice-daily mixed insulin is specifically not offered to newly diagnosed adults.
whyNot.1: Basal-only regimens are not offered; meals need bolus cover.
whyNot.3: Bolus-only leaves no background insulin, risking ketosis between meals.

A.q: A woman with type 1 diabetes has HbA1c 52 mmol/mol and no problematic hypoglycaemia. What HbA1c should the nurse encourage her to aim for, as advised by NICE?
A.why: NICE NG17 rec 1.6.6: support adults with type 1 diabetes to aim for HbA1c 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or lower, agreed individually.

whyNot.0: 58 mmol/mol is the NG28 type 2 level at which medicines are intensified.
whyNot.1: 53 mmol/mol is the level services audit against (NG17 1.6.9) and the NG28 type 2 target on hypo-causing drugs; it is not the NG17 aim.
whyNot.2: 64 mmol/mol is above any NICE target.

B.q: Mr Petrov has erratic glucose readings and firm, rubbery lumps at the abdominal sites where he injects every day. What is the most likely cause and action?
B.why: NICE NG17 recs 1.7.19 and 1.7.21: rotate injection sites and avoid repeated injection at the same point; check sites when control changes. Lumps of lipohypertrophy absorb insulin erratically.

whyNot.1: Firm painless lumps from repeated injection are not allergy, and insulin must not be stopped in type 1 diabetes.
whyNot.2: No signs of infection (heat, redness, fever) are described.
whyNot.3: Increasing the dose into lumpy tissue risks unpredictable hypoglycaemia once he rotates sites.

B.q: At her annual review, Mrs Holt reports she no longer feels shaky when her glucose is low. Which tool should the nurse use to quantify her hypoglycaemia awareness?
B.why: NICE NG17 recs 1.9.1–1.9.2: assess hypoglycaemia awareness at each annual review using the Gold score or Clarke score.

whyNot.3: Rockall scores the risk after upper GI bleeding.

B.q: A man with type 1 diabetes uses capillary blood glucose monitoring. What is the minimum testing NICE advises on a routine day?
options: Twice a day, morning and evening
Once a day at varied times
B.why: NICE NG17 rec 1.6.19: measure at least 4 times a day, including before each meal and before bed.

whyNot.0: Twice daily misses pre-meal readings needed to adjust bolus doses.
whyNot.1: A single fasting reading cannot guide mealtime insulin.
whyNot.3: Once a day is far below the NG17 minimum.

C.q: Ms Ahmed, 41, has type 1 diabetes and impaired hypoglycaemia awareness despite completing structured education. She asks if she should run her glucose higher to stay safe. Which response best reflects NICE NG17?
options: Yes, aim for 8–12 mmol/L before meals
Yes, let HbA1c rise to around 64 mmol/mol
Stop bolus insulin on days with lows
Keep targets; review insulin, consider CGM or pump
C.why: NICE NG17 recs 1.9.6–1.9.8: avoid relaxing individualised targets for impaired awareness; review insulin regimen and doses, reinforce education, and offer an insulin pump or real-time CGM.

whyNot.0: NG17 says avoid relaxing blood glucose targets to address impaired awareness.
whyNot.1: Allowing HbA1c to rise is relaxing targets and increases long-term complications.
whyNot.2: Stopping bolus insulin risks hyperglycaemia and ketosis.

C.q: Mr Osei's wife finds him drowsy and unable to swallow safely; his meter reads 2.4 mmol/L. She has been trained to give glucagon. After giving IM glucagon, what should happen next?
options: Give a second dose of glucagon at 5 minutes
Give him a sugary drink straight away
C.why: NICE NG17 rec 1.9.11: after IM glucagon, check for response at 10 minutes; give IV glucose if consciousness is not improving, then oral carbohydrate when safe.

whyNot.1: NG17 does not advise a repeat glucagon at 5 minutes; failure to improve needs IV glucose.
whyNot.2: He cannot swallow safely, so oral drinks risk aspiration.
whyNot.3: An hour is too long; response is checked at 10 minutes.

C.q: Mr Jensen, 22, has type 1 diabetes and gastroenteritis. His glucose is 16 mmol/L and he has stopped his long-acting insulin because he is not eating. What is the most important advice?
options: Stop all insulin until he is eating
Restart basal insulin and check ketones
Drink sugary fluids to raise intake
Halve his basal dose and avoid testing
C.why: NICE NG17 rec 1.10.1: ketone monitoring is part of sick-day rules. People with type 1 diabetes still need basal insulin when ill or not eating, because without it they make ketones and can develop DKA.

whyNot.0: Stopping insulin in type 1 diabetes leads to ketosis and DKA.
whyNot.2: His glucose is already high; he needs fluids and insulin, not extra sugar.
whyNot.3: Reducing insulin and not testing removes the safety checks sick-day rules depend on.

reteach.title: A car that needs two pedals
reteach.question: Think of insulin in type 1 diabetes like the two pedals that keep a car steady on a hill. What are they?

blocks.body: Basal insulin is the gentle, constant pressure that stops the car rolling backwards: it covers background needs all day and night, even when not eating. Bolus insulin is the extra push for each meal. Take the basal foot off and the car rolls back into ketosis. Targets tell you if the pressure is right: 5–7 on waking, 4–7 before meals, HbA1c 48 or lower.

blocks.text: Not eating does not mean no insulin. Stopping basal insulin in type 1 diabetes leads to DKA.

explain.body: Typical (not universal) features: ketosis, rapid weight loss, onset under 50, BMI below 25, personal or family autoimmune disease. Do not use age or BMI alone to diagnose or exclude it. Measure diabetes-specific autoantibodies.

test.q: A 58-year-old with a BMI of 28 presents with hyperglycaemia, ketosis and rapid weight loss. What does NICE say about using age and BMI here?
test.why: NICE NG17 rec 1.1.2: do not use age or BMI alone to exclude or diagnose type 1 diabetes. Ketosis and rapid weight loss are typical type 1 features.

whyNot.0: Onset under 50 is typical, not required.
whyNot.1: BMI under 25 is typical, but a higher BMI does not confirm type 2.
whyNot.3: They are clues, not diagnostic criteria.

explain.body: HbA1c 48 mmol/mol or lower, individualised. Capillary glucose 5–7 on waking, 4–7 before meals, 5–9 at least 90 minutes after meals if tested.

test.q: A man with type 1 diabetes tests 2 hours after lunch and gets 8.2 mmol/L. How does this compare with the NICE post-meal target?
options: Above the 4–7 range, so too high
Above the 5–7 range, so too high
test.why: NICE NG17 rec 1.6.23: 5–9 mmol/L at least 90 minutes after eating. 8.2 is within range.

whyNot.3: 8.2 is far above the 4.0 hypoglycaemia threshold.

explain.body: Basal-bolus multiple daily injections are the regimen of choice. Rotate sites and avoid repeated injections at the same point. Check sites at least annually and whenever control changes.

test.q: How often does NICE advise that injection sites are checked in adults with type 1 diabetes?
test.why: NICE NG17 rec 1.7.21: check injection site condition at least annually and whenever new problems with glucose control occur.

whyNot.0: 3 years is too long; lipohypertrophy can develop within months.
whyNot.2: HbA1c is usually checked 3–6 monthly; NG17 sets an annual minimum for sites.
whyNot.3: Checks are routine, not left to the person to request.

explain.body: Assess hypo awareness every year using the Gold or Clarke score. Do not relax targets for unawareness. Ketone monitoring is part of sick-day rules, and basal insulin continues during illness.

test.q: Which is part of NICE sick-day rules for adults with type 1 diabetes?
test.why: NICE NG17 rec 1.10.1: consider ketone monitoring (blood or urine) as part of sick-day rules.

whyNot.1: Insulin is continued; stopping it causes DKA.
whyNot.2: Fluids are needed to avoid dehydration.
whyNot.3: Oral glucose-lowering tablets cannot replace insulin in type 1 diabetes.
